text.0_, 0_Siman, 0_Paragraph: With G-D's Help I will begin to explain the reasons of the [Jewish] customs according to what the Sages taught us, the way that we should follow in.
text.0_, 0_Siman, 1_Paragraph: The Reason: that [the Sages] established ritual washing in the morning is because that in the morning we are made anew, like it says, "They are renewed every morning." Therefore they established ritual washing at this time. (Beis Yosef 4) Another Reason: because an impure spirit rests on them. (Zohar Parshas Vayeshev)
text.0_, 0_Siman, 2_Paragraph: Footnote: Because an impure spirit rests on them. See Shaarei Teshuva 1:1, "In the Birkei Yosef it is written that if it happens that the water is far away and their is no one to bring it to you, some of those who possess sensitivity [in halakha] are accustomed to walk less then four cubits at a time. However, this is not proper and it is better to hurry in order that the impure spirit should not stay a while on your hands." And in the Ateres Zekanim 4 it is written in the name of the Zohar that one who walks 4 cubits in the morning before ritually washing is deserving of death. And in the book Agra D'Parka 9 it is written, in the name of the old and beloved Holy Grandfather [in the name] of Rabbi Moshe Zechut of blessed memory, about the prohibition of walking 4 cubits without ritual washing in the morning, that one should be careful to not place his feet on the ground without ritual washing otherwise, G-D forbid, all the evil spirits that are in the animalistic soul will chase after him to incite him. And this is hinted in the verse, "He is set on the path of no good," Therefore, G-D forbid, "He does not reject evil." And over there [in the Agra D'Parka] a reason is written for this, [which is] because the longer the disgusting spirit rests on mans hand he should not give it any measure of importance. And see the Shulchan Aruch HaRav 4:2 that [states that] "one needs to be very careful to not touch any food or drinks before ritually washing so that he does not contaminate them. And we are accustomed to be lenient about the touch of children that have not been trained [in Jewish practice] because a holy spirit has not entered into them yet. And also a non-jews touch we are not concered about. And one wo is careful about a child's touch from the day of his circumcision and onwards, it is said about him that he is holy...." And about if one is allowed to make a blessing facing the waters which he washed with, it is written in the Birkei Yosef "that the custom of those who are stringent about G-D's words is to not read [a Torah verse] or make a blessing in front of it. And in the book Avodas Hakodesh it is written, one should cover the vessel that contains the water which was used to ritually wash his hands because these waters are impure, and they are more [impure] than urine. and in the Zohar Parshas Vayeishev pg. 184 it is written, do not let the impure water tarry in the house." And in the book Nachalah L'Yisrael it is written, "I heard from the Genius and Holy Master from Sanz of blessed memory that the author of the Avodas Hakodesh retracted from what he wrote that it is forbidden to recite [Torah verses] in front of [impure water]." And in the book Eshel Avraham by the Holy Genius from Buchach of blessed memory, siman 4, writes that such water would be nullified in a large mixture. And [it is said] in the name of the Holy Genius, the Master Rav Sholom from Belz of blessed memory, "One who lifts from inside the house the vessel with the water which was used for ritual washing in the morning and spills it outside has the capacity to fear G-D." Therefore it is good to reduce frivolity in the house, whatever is possible. It is written in the Kav Hayashar pg. 83, "Those of [worthy] deed are accustomed to say the following prayer after ritually washing their hands: 'To the G-D of the spirits, may it be your will, Hashem my G-D and the G-D of my forefathers, that the merit of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob should stand for us to save us and all of our descendents from any transgression and sin inorder to uphold the commandment of your holy Torah without any foreign thoughts, and purify our hearts to serve you with truth and with perfection, Amen. And this prayer should not be taken lightly for I found it in the authorship of an early Rabbi from the days of Rashi of blessed memory that [the prayer] was received by him, because after the Temple was destroyed and sacrifices ceased, prayer took the place of sacrifice to awaken divine mercy upon us... and it is good to say this prayer immediatly after the blessing on ritual hand washing, because that is a time of good will and divine mercy, and hints to the merit of Torah and the merit of our forefathers.
text.0_, 1_Siman, 0_Paragraph: The Reason: that when one awakens he needs to pour water on each hand three times is because, [doing things] three times creates a status quo and continues in that [new] status. However, for other matters involving washing, one time is enough to work. (Seder HaYom):*And these [are the] matters which obligate washing with water: getting up from bed, leaving the bathroom or bathhouse, etc. one who does any of these things and does not wash his hands, if he is learned he will forget his learning and if he is not learned he will go insane (Orach Chayim 4). The Eliya Rabah writes there, "on this that it is written, '[one who is not learned will go insane' I heard that [this means] that he will come to sin, because a person does not sin unless a foolish spirit enters him." An in the book Kav Hayashar it is written that anyone who is careful with these, above-mentioned washings, sin won't come to him easily. And anyone who is not careful with them, the impure forces (lit. husks) which rule in the disgusting places surround him. However, by ritually washing it is certain that these impure forces will distance themselves from that man. And about one who exits the bathroom, the Magen Avraham 200:17 writes that one doesn't need to pour water on his hands three times, but in 7:1, he writes in the name of the Zohar that one needs to pour three times, and [the Magen Avraham] differs from that. And see the Shaarei Teshuva 4:20 that writes,
text.0_, 10_Siman, 1_Paragraph:
The final notebook:
And one needs to cover the head: See Taz 3 on [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chaim] Section 8, that one should be careful and not be bareheaded even outside of prayer [times], since the people understand it as lightheadedness and licentiousness. And it is fully forbidden now that it has become a practice among the idolaters always, as soon as they sit down, to remove the hat. And, if so, it is included in the category of and you shall not follow their customs [Leviticus 18:3], see there. And at the end of Shabbat [156b], "Cover your head so that you will have the fear of Your master upon you." And likewise, in Kiddushin 33a, "A certain man passed before him and did not cover his head. They said, 'How rude is this man, etc.'" And it is found in Tractate Kallah about a certain infant who passed by the elders and his head was uncovered [that] Rabbi Eliezer said he was a mamzer, and Rabbi Yehudah said he was the son of a menstruant, and Rabbi Akiva said that he was a mamzer and the son of a menstruant. So he asked his mother, and she admitted to him that it was so. Hence one should distance himself from this more than from their other practices, see there.
And see Bekhor Shor (Shabbat), who wrote, "I have seen those that are exacting, [that] even in the bathhouse, they place a cloth over the head. And I have practiced this from my youth," see there, and also see below in the addenda to Paragraph 249.
And in the book, Tzemach David, Part II, in the Fourth Millenium, he wrote, and these are his [words]: At the beginning of the Greek empire, there was a sage in Athens, the city of wisdom, and some say in Rome, and he would expound in public that people should remove their hats from upon their heads when they were working. And his reason was that earlier, the greatest humility was from those who would walk barefoot, like the matter that is stated, and he was walking barefoot (II Samuel 15:30). But since the head is more honored than the feet, there is more humility in showing the head than from showing the feet. And it is from this that the custom spread that someone lesser than his fellow, or even similar to him, should humble himself by showing and baring his head. However, this custom is only [found] among the Christians and not with anyone besides them. To here [are his words].
text.0_, 36_Siman, 0_Paragraph: The reason: Regarding the matter of blessing, that at the beginning, one speaks to God as if he is in front of Him, but in the end as if he is not in front of Him, it is because it is stated (Psalms 16:8), "I have set the Lord always before me."*In the Zohar Chai on Genesis, p. 168, he writes as follows: My holy teacher, our master the rabbi, our Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heshel of Apta testified about our holy rabbi, our master, Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin, that he would not even raise his eyelids without unifying [God's] name, all the more so [with] speech and all the more so [with] a response. And once my master, my beloved, the holy one, said, "I was walking to the house of prayer with very enlightening tefillin, and I heard that they were calling in front of me, 'Give honor to his son, etc.' But when I came back from the house of prayer, I was holding a tobacco pipe without intent. And I heard them calling, 'Woe to x, who is rebelling against his Master.'" As so is it found in the Tosefta, "A person should not use face or his feet except for the glory of his Maker (Konehu)" - he should 'make' (koneh) and unify Him (Hu, which also refers to a name of God); in the same way as, "in all of your ways, know Him (Hu)." And with righteous people like these, the shells will be finished, and it will be a favorable time. So when he mentions the name and says, "Blessed are You, Lord," it is as if he is in front of Him; but when he says, afterward, "our God, King of the world," it comes out that he is not standing in front of Him. As it means to say [that] this God of ours, who is the King of the world, He has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to do them (Abudarham). And see the Shibulei HaLeket, Law 168: "I have set the Lord always before me." Rav said, "Blessed are You." Shmuel said, "Blessed is He." Hence, our Rabbis established it like both of them - "Blessed are You," like Rav, and "who sanctified us," like Shmuel. See there.
text.0_, 846_Siman, 0_Paragraph: The reason that the miracle of Ḥanukkah is not mentioned at all in the Mishnah is that our holy Rabbi [Judah the Prince], the compiler of the Mishnah, was from the line of King David, peace be upon him. And the miracle of Ḥanukkah was done by the Hasmoneans, who seized the kingship and were not of the line of David. And this was bad for our holy Rabbi, so as he wrote the Mishnah according to the holy spirit, the miracle was dropped from its composition. This is in the name of the holy genius, the author of the Ḥatam Sofer, may his righteous and holy memory be for a blessing.
text.0_, 866_Siman, 0_Paragraph: The Reason for the Four Parshiot (Special Torah Readings) Three of them are in memory of the time that the Temple existed. And they are Parshat Shekalim, Parshat Parah Adumah and Parshat HaChodesh. For we announce [the obligation of] the shekel payment on the first of Adar. As the Torah stated (Numbers 28:14), "that shall be the monthly burnt offering for each new moon of the year." And from the oral tradition, they learned that it is meaning to say [it is to be] from the first of the month [of Nissan]. And it said monthly (bechodsho, which is related to the word for new), meaning to say, renovate and offer a sacrifice from the contribution of the new shekel coins. Hence we announce [it] one month before Nissan, so that each one can prepare his half [shekel coin], and all will be collected and brought to the Temple with the arrival of Nissan. And so when Adar begins during the days of the week, we bring up the announcement to the Shabbat before it. As if we delay it to the next Shabbat, there will not be a complete month until Rosh Chodesh (the first day of) Nissan. But when Rosh Chodesh Adar is on Shabbat, there is no need to bring it up, since there is surely a [whole] month. And with Parshat Parah Adumah, it is to inform the people that are impure from [contact with] the dead that they should purify themselves with the ashes of the heifer. For the distant ones began to go up to Jerusalem on the first day of Nissan. Hence we do not take a break between Parshat Parah and Parshat HaChodesh. And Parshat HaChodesh is to inform the people that the first day of Nissan will be in the coming week, so that they will prepare themselves for the pilgrimage to the festival. And Parshat Zakhor The Pri Meggadim wrote (282:3), "Even though a minor counts for the tally of seven (that read from the Torah on Shabbat) and, in the time of the Talmud, a minor would go up and read on his own, a minor that goes up for Parshat Zakhor should not read [it] on his own. For behold there are some that say that the reading of Parshat Zakhor is [mandated[ by the Torah, so we would not fulfill [the commandment] with the reading of a minor. And see Taz 685:2." is because of Purim. As Haman came from the seed of Amalek, and the Torah stated (Deuteronomy 25:17), "Remember what Amalek did to you." And from the oral tradition, they learned that remembering is oral, etc. And we say in the Yerushalmi, "It is proper that we should bring forward Parshat HaChodesh before Parshat Parah Adumah, since the tabernacle was established on the first of Nissan, and they burned the heifer on the second of it. So why did they say to bring forward the red heifer? Because it is the purification of the Jewish people, meaning from the impurity of the dead, so that they will not be pushed off until the Second Pesach." Abudarham.
text.2_Segulot, 89_Section, 0_Paragraph:
A charm [segulah] for pregnancy and raising children:
A woman who is forlorn about raising [her] children or who doesn't have any at all, God forbid, should say the haftarah of the first day of Rosh Hashanah [the story of Hannah miraculously giving birth to Samuel] after she lights candles [at the onset of Shabbat]. She should also give a few coins to charity before lighting the candles, though every woman should do that. And through this, they will merit to have proper children who are Torah scholars. [From] the book, Shaarei Emunah, in the name of the book, Zer Zahav, that there is a tradition about this in the holy city of Jerusalem from Ari, may his memory be blessed.
